title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with generated video, not a model error inside a deployed product. The caller appeared on a WhatsApp video call as a named public official and used that appearance to open a request for money. A second person then posed as a CBI official, which added the weight of an enforcement agency to the same request. The channel was a consumer messaging app, and the only check available to the recipient was his own judgement of the face and voice on the screen.

Catching it would have required confirming the caller's identity outside the call, through an official office or channel, because a convincing live video leaves nothing inside the call for the recipient to verify. It would also have required reading the sequence of fees, exchange charges, PIN unlocking and a fine as one script rather than as separate legitimate demands. Nothing in the reporting indicates that any such check existed in the channel or was offered to the recipient.

What is not established is who produced the deepfake, whether the person posing as the CBI official also used generated media, and whether any arrest or recovery of the money followed. A case registered under the Information Technology Act is an allegation, not a finding.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29 year old Bengaluru security guard, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on September 9. The caller used an AI generated deepfake to pose as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay and offered financial aid. The fraudster said Giri would get Rs 11 lakh, later claiming Rs 5 lakh was allotted. A supposed manager then asked for fees, including Rs 5,000 as exchange charges and Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN.

Giri initially paid Rs 18,000. Another person posing as a CBI official demanded more than Rs 50,000 as a fine. Fearing loss of earlier payments, Giri sent more money, totaling over Rs 1.04 lakh. When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, he refused and realized he had been cheated. He contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then Byappanahalli police. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act. Police urged people not to trust such calls or make payments based on them.
